name: Hongshan culture
title: The story of the Hongshan culture

text: About 6,700 years ago, the Hongshan people lived in northeast China, in lands from Inner Mongolia to Liaoning.
Back then their land had deep lakes and forests, not the desert it is today.
src: The Hongshan culture was a Neolithic culture of the West Liao river basin in northeast China, with sites from Inner Mongolia to Liaoning dated from about 4700 to 2900 BCE
The land was not then the desert it is now. / from 12,000 to 4,000 years ago the region had deep lakes, forests and rich aquatic resources

text: They were farmers who grew millet, a small grain.
In later times, millet made up most of what they ate.
src: the Hongshan people grew millet, broomcorn millet in particular
up to 80% in the Late Hongshan

text: They were in touch with farmers by the Yellow River, who passed on stone knives for harvesting.
Some farmers from farther south moved north and became part of the Hongshan people.
src: lived beside the Yangshao culture of the Yellow River, and the two interacted / Stone harvesting knives of Yangshao origin reached Haminmangha
millet farmers from Henan and Shandong helped to form the Hongshan people, moving north by inland and coastal routes

text: At Niuheliang they built an underground temple with painted walls and clay figures up to three times as big as people.
A clay head with eyes of jade gave it the name Goddess Temple.
src: an underground temple complex with an altar / The temple, about a metre below ground, was built of stone platforms with painted walls and murals / clay figures as large as three times life size
Archaeologists named it the “Goddess Temple” after a clay female head with eyes inlaid with jade.

text: They built tombs of stone, covered them with mounds of stones and often placed jade objects inside.
Their jade pig dragons are some of the earliest jade carvings known, and small copper rings have been found too.
src: More than 60 nearby tombs were built of stone and covered by stone mounds, often with jade objects inside.
Its burials hold some of the earliest known examples of jade working, among them the jade pig dragons / Small copper rings have also been excavated.

text: The Hongshan culture ended about 4,900 years ago, and later a changing climate turned the lakes and forests into desert.
Their jade and tombs remain, and they are believed to have helped shape early Chinese civilisation.
src: c. 2900 BCE: The Hongshan culture comes to an end / Climate change that began about 4,200 years ago turned the region’s lakes and forests into desert
see the Hongshan culture as an important stage of early Chinese civilisation, and it is believed to have influenced its development
